title: Get through winter in one heated room
summary: Pick one small room, close it off without closing off your way out, heat the people and the beds rather than the air, and keep a stove going safely overnight. What kills people here is fire and carbon monoxide in a closed-up room, and burns from contact heat on people who cannot feel them.

materials.item: Blankets, drapes, tarps or shower curtains for doorways, windows and a canopy over the bed
Closed-cell foam, camping mats or gym mats for under the beds
Insulation board or batts for windows you can give up
Rubber hot-water bottle with cover, or a bottle rated for boiling water

steps.text: Pick one small room on the sheltered, sunny side, with few outside walls and windows, a low ceiling, and a chimney flue if you will burn anything (MU Extension, Be Ready Utah, CMHC wood heat).
steps.warn: A basement is warmer, but propane collects there (WorkSafeNB propane), CO from any burner can build up, it is damp, and it may have only the stairs as a way out.

steps.text: Before you seal anything, pick the way out: one window that opens from inside and one door, both kept clear of boards, bars and snow (Miami-Dade bars).
steps.warn: People die in fires behind boarded and barred windows (NFPA bars 1994, Firehouse Homestead).

steps.text: Fit a smoke alarm near the ceiling by the exit and a CO alarm in the room, and put an ABC extinguisher by the stove or heater (CMHC wood heat).
steps.warn: The CO alarm test button checks the electronics and horn, not the sensor (First Alert test). Check its temperature range and expiry date on the label.

steps.text: Close off the rest of the house: shut doors, hang blankets over doorways, and stuff the gaps under doors (CDC winter, MU Extension). Keep blankets, cardboard and partitions well clear of any stove, pipe or heater, and leave the exit door free to open.

Cover the windows at night with blankets or curtains, and open the sunny ones by day (Be Ready Utah, CDC winter). Hang covers loose so one pull brings them down: never nailed or taped over the escape window, and well clear of any stove, pipe or heater.
Insulate the floor and get the beds off it, with foam, blankets or cardboard under every sleeper (Manitoba cold).
Pitch a tent or build a blanket den over the beds, well clear of any stove, pipe or heater (Be Ready Utah).
steps.warn: Never a candle, lamp or stove inside a tent (CPSC camping). Keep heaters out too: tent fabric and bedding burn, and a small air space fills with CO (CPSC ODS).

steps.text: Dress in several thin layers with a hat and dry socks, and change any damp base layer as soon as you stop working (UKHSA keep warm, CCOHS cold working).
Warm beds with hot-water bottles filled with boiled water cooled a few minutes, no more than two-thirds full, in a cover (Swansea Bay bottles).
steps.warn: No bottle or pad in bed for babies, people with numb feet, anyone very cold or frail, or anyone who may sleep too deeply to wake from heat (drink, sedatives): they burn without knowing it (Lullaby winter, COBIS bottles, AAFP burns).

steps.text: If you burn fuel for heat, use only appliances made for indoor use, follow the label, and keep a window open about 2.5 cm (1 in) (MU Extension, CPSC 5052).
steps.warn: Never a grill, charcoal, camp stove, generator or gas oven for heat (CDC winter, Get Prepared outages), even though some older guides allow them with ventilation.

steps.text: Move warm air down from the ceiling: a ceiling fan on low turning clockwise, or a small fan in the top of a doorway (ENERGY STAR fans, CMHC wood heat).
For the night, rake the stove coals forward, load larger pieces close together, burn hot until charred, then turn the air down in stages (CMHC wood heat).
steps.warn: Never choke it to a smoulder: that builds creosote for a chimney fire and makes CO.

steps.text: Set a fire watch: one person awake at a time, in turns (MU Extension).
Charge lithium on a hard surface away from the exit while someone is awake, and keep flooded lead-acid out of the sleeping room (LFB charging, CCOHS battery charging).
steps.warn: Check the pack's charging range (one maker allows +5 to +50 °C) and let a cold pack warm up in the room before charging it.

steps.text: Drain the plumbing in the rest of the house if it will freeze, and check often on anyone at risk (Get Prepared outages, CDC winter).

notes:
## Which room

Heat one small room well, not the whole house badly. Confine emergency heat to a small area and keep its doors shut (MU Extension).

- **Small.** Less air and wall to heat.
- **On the warm side.** Pick the side of the house away from the prevailing wind (MU Extension). A south-facing room takes in sun by day (Be Ready Utah, MU Extension): open the covers then, close them at dusk (CDC winter), and see [Solar air heater](#guides/build_solar_air_heater).
- **Few outside walls and windows.** Avoid rooms with big windows or uninsulated walls. An interior bathroom probably loses the least heat and air (MU Extension).
- **A low ceiling.** Heat from any heater rises and collects at the ceiling (CMHC wood heat).
- **A chimney, if you'll burn anything.** A stove should go on a proper chimney flue (CMHC wood heat). Never run a stovepipe out through a window, wall or ceiling without the right thimble or listed pass-through: see [Install a wood stove](#guides/build_stove_install).
- **Room for every bed** well away from any heater: at least 1 m (3 ft) from a portable heater (Simcoe Muskoka), and at least the label clearance from a stove, which CMHC puts at 1,200 mm (48 in) for an uncertified radiant stove (CMHC wood heat). See [Safe indoor heating](#ref/reference_fire_heat/safe_indoor_heating).

### The basement trade-off
- **For:** the earth around it keeps it warmer than the floors above (MU Extension).
- **Against:** propane is heavier than air and collects in basements (WorkSafeNB propane). Carbon monoxide builds up there too: a basement is not "outside" (see [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide)). A stove in a basement with a long pipe run, several elbows and a chimney up an outside wall is almost certain to spill smoke (CMHC wood heat). Basements are damp: see [Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation). And many have only the stairs as a way out.

## Shrink the space

- Close off rooms you don't need. Stuff towels or rags in the gaps under doors (CDC winter).
- Hang blankets, drapes or shower curtains over doorways and windows, especially at night. Cardboard or plywood partitions block draughts (MU Extension). Blankets, cardboard and plywood burn: keep them clear of the stove, pipe and any heater, at the label or code clearance (CMHC wood heat). Never block the window you will escape through; hang its cover loose.
- The air is coldest near the floor (Manitoba cold). Put rugs, foam or flattened cardboard down, and get beds and feet up off the floor.
- Keep everyone in the one room. Sharing a bed keeps people warm, especially children (MU Extension), but not babies: a baby sleeps alone in its own crib, cradle or bassinet in your room (Health Canada safe sleep).
- Don't make it airtight. Breath and cooking fill a sealed room with damp ([Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation)), and anything that burns needs fresh air. When a heater runs, open windows about 2.5 cm (1 in) on opposite sides of the room (MU Extension).

### A tent inside the room
A tent pitched in the warm room, or a den of blankets over the bed, holds body heat close (Be Ready Utah). Use it for sleeping only. **No heater, candle, lamp or stove inside it, ever:**
- Treat tents and sleeping bags as flammable, and pitch the tent or den well clear of any stove, pipe or heater. Candles in tents have caused serious and fatal burns, and CPSC says never to take a stove, lantern or candle inside a tent (CPSC camping).
- A small space runs short of air fast. Indoor-rated propane heaters carry a sensor that shuts them off when the oxygen in a tent or camper falls below 18%; older heaters without one have killed people in tents and campers (CPSC ODS).
- Every flame makes CO, and a tent holds it around your head.

Leave the door or a vent open a little so your breath doesn't soak the bedding (see [Tarp shelter](#guides/build_tarp_shelter), Mistakes).

## Keep a way out

Closing up a room for warmth is how people get trapped in a fire.
- A good escape plan has two ways out of every room (Miami-Dade bars). In the warm room that means the door and a window that opens. Bars need a quick-release that opens from inside with no key, special knowledge or excessive force (Miami-Dade bars).
- People die behind bars and boards. In the US, fire deaths blamed on illegal security bars and locks rose from under one a year (1980–85) to nearly 16 a year (1986–91) (NFPA bars 1994). In Homestead, Florida, plywood left between the windows and burglar bars trapped heat and smoke in a fire that killed five (Firehouse Homestead).
- So in the warm room, leave one window that opens from inside, and keep the door clear. Shovel both from outside after every snowfall. Where you can, lay the room out so nobody must pass the stove or a heater to reach the door or window. Make sure everyone can open them, and practise (Miami-Dade bars).
- Fit a smoke alarm on or near the ceiling at the room's exit, a CO alarm (CMHC puts it at or near ceiling level), and keep an ABC extinguisher near the stove or heater (CMHC wood heat, Simcoe Muskoka). CO alarms have limits: their test button checks the horn, not the sensor; read [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).

## Heat the person, not the air

- In a cold house, bed may be the safest, warmest place for short spells (MU Extension).
- Several thin layers keep you warmer than one thick one (UKHSA keep warm). Eat well-balanced meals and drink warm sweet drinks or broth. Skip alcohol: it makes you lose heat faster (CDC winter).
- A hat that covers the ears (CCOHS cold working). Dry socks; with two pairs, the outer one a size bigger so the inner isn't squeezed (CCOHS cold working).
- Clothes and bedding to scavenge: see [Where to find warm clothing](#guides/reference_where_warm_clothing).

### The bed
- **What's under you matters.** Sleeping-bag ratings are measured with the bag on a foam mat (Rab ratings). Put closed-cell foam, folded blankets or layers of cardboard under the bag, thicker than seems sensible ([Tarp shelter](#guides/build_tarp_shelter), Ground insulation).
- **Two bags or more blankets** beat one, if the outer layer is loose: compressed insulation stops working (CCOHS cold working).
- **Air it every day.** Hang bedding open in the warm room while you're up so the night's moisture dries out ([Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation)).

### Sleeping-bag ratings (EN ISO 23537)

| Rating | What it means (Rab ratings) |
|---|---|
| Comfort | Lowest temperature to sleep relaxed through the night |
| Limit | Lowest temperature to sleep through the night curled up |
| Extreme | Emergency only: up to six hours curled up, and frostbite is very possible |

Plan on the comfort figure. The extreme figure is a survival line, not a sleeping temperature. The standard doesn't measure below −20 °C (−4 °F) (Rab ratings).

## Contact heat

Warmth on the skin goes straight to the person, but it burns people who can't feel it or move away. **No contact heat in bed for:** babies (no hot-water bottle in a baby's sleep space, Lullaby winter; electric blankets aren't safe for babies, Tasmania Fire bedrooms); people with numb feet or reduced feeling, as with diabetes, neuropathy, spina bifida or cerebral palsy, who are told to take extra care (Swansea Bay bottles, COBIS bottles); anyone very cold, whose skin burns easily (WMS-Hypo); and anyone frail, drunk or sedated, who may not wake or move away. Alcohol and sedatives are linked to serious burns in older adults (AAFP burns); no source names them for bottles, so that part is a precaution.

### Hot-water bottles
- Use a rubber bottle made for it (marked BS 1970), checked for perished rubber, cracks and leaks each time. Replace it every two years (Swansea Bay bottles).
- Fill with boiled water left to cool for a few minutes, never more than two-thirds full. Squeeze the air out and screw the stopper tight (Swansea Bay bottles, COBIS bottles). An adult fills it, never a child (COBIS bottles).
- Always in a cover. Not against one patch of skin for more than 20 minutes, and never sit or lie on it (Swansea Bay bottles). Warm the bed with it, then take it out before you get in (Tasmania Fire bedrooms).
- A hard bottle works if its maker rates it for the heat. Nalgene rates its Sustain (Renew) bottles for boiling water and its HDPE bottles for about 82–93 °C (180–200 °F). Wait a few seconds before closing the lid, because steam builds pressure, and don't rest it against bare skin (Nalgene hot water).

### Warmed bricks and stones
A brick or dense stone warmed beside the stove holds its heat well, but it has no thermostat and can be far hotter than cooled bottle water. No source we opened covers this, so it is our judgement: warm it gently beside the stove, not on the top plate, handle it with gloves or tongs, wrap it in thick cloth, and keep it from the people above. Use only dry ones that have sat indoors: a science-news article says river and lake stones can hold water that turns to steam and bursts them, citing no study (IFLScience rocks).

### 12 V pads and blankets
An electric blanket may stave off hypothermia even in a poorly heated house (MMWR chronic); the no-contact-heat list applies to pads too. A 12 V car blanket or pad heats one person for a small fraction of what a room heater needs: see [Electric blanket teardown](#guides/teardown_electric_blanket) and [Power budget](#guides/reference_power_budget). Run it from a battery charged by solar, with a fuse in the positive lead near the battery ([Wiring 12 V systems](#guides/skill_dc_wiring)). Read the amps on the plug and fuse for that. Switch it off or put it on a timer once the bed is warm. Never fold or bunch it while it's on. Never on frostbitten skin (CDC hypothermia).

## Stay dry

The trap is sweating while you haul wood or shovel, then sitting still in damp clothes.
- Open up before you get hot: gloves, hat and scarf off, jacket open, then outer layers off (CCOHS cold working).
- Clothing next to the skin gets wet and its insulation drops sharply (CCOHS cold working). Change the damp base layer and socks as soon as you stop.
- Cotton gets damp fast and stops insulating. Wool and synthetics keep some warmth when wet (CCOHS cold working).
- Dry wet things in the warm room, never on the stove or heater: at least the label clearance from a stove, 1 m (3 ft) from a portable heater ([Safe indoor heating](#ref/reference_fire_heat/safe_indoor_heating)).

## Move the heat down and around

Warm air rises to the ceiling, spreads across it, falls down the walls and comes back along the floor. These currents are slow (CMHC wood heat).
- **Ceiling fan:** in winter run it on low, turning clockwise, to push warm ceiling air down (ENERGY STAR fans, CMHC wood heat).
- **Doorways:** the wall above an interior door blocks warm air at ceiling level. A small fan in the top corner of a doorway moves heat to the next room (CMHC wood heat). Leave open the door to where the beds are.

## Candles and flower-pot heaters: honest numbers

- NIST measured a burning taper candle at 77 W, give or take 9 W (NIST candles). A small electric room heater is 1,000–2,000 W ([Power budget](#guides/reference_power_budget)), so you'd need 13 to 26 candles to match one, each an open flame to watch.
- A clay pot over candles adds no heat. It only soaks up and spreads the same 80 W or so a candle gives (AAP FactCheck). One set a home on fire in Derby, England, in November 2022, and about 50 people had to leave the building (AAP FactCheck).
- Keep candles at least 30 cm (12 in) from anything that burns, and put them out when you leave or sleep (USFA candles). Don't burn anything bigger than candles indoors without venting to outside (MU Extension). See [Candles](#guides/safety_candles).

## Overnight with a wood stove

The aim is a fire that's still flaming, just slower, not one choked down to smoke (CMHC wood heat, BC wood burning).
1. Before bed, clear a little ash from the front and rake the live coals forward, towards the air inlet.
2. Load larger pieces, packed close together, on and behind the coals.
3. Open the air fully until the firebox is full of flame and the outer pieces are charred: 5 to 20 minutes says CMHC, 15 to 30 says BC, depending on the load and how dry the wood is.
4. Turn the air down in stages. The wood should still be flaming after the last turn-down.
5. In the morning, rake the coals forward again and reload.

**Never let it smoulder.** A smouldering fire wastes wood, spills smoke when the door is opened, and lays down black, tarry creosote, the kind that feeds chimney fires. With older stoves, in bad cases, enough creosote for a damaging chimney fire builds up in a few weeks, so check the chimney often until you know your rate (CMHC wood heat). A bed of glowing charcoal makes CO even with no smoke, so the flue must be sound all night (CMHC wood heat). See [Chimney sweeping](#guides/skill_chimney_sweeping), [Test a chimney](#guides/test_chimney) and [What to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn).

**Keep a fire watch.** One person should stay awake to watch for fire and for poor ventilation. Drowsiness is a sign of CO (MU Extension). Take turns, and wake the next person rather than dozing off. Ashes go outside in a lidded metal can stood on concrete, never indoors or on a wooden deck: they stay hot for days and give off CO (CMHC wood heat).

## Other heat in the room

- Fuel heaters only if made for indoor use, read and followed from the label, with the window cracked and the CO alarm working. Refuel only outdoors, with the heater off and cold (CPSC 5052). See [Heater labels](#guides/reference_heater_labels), [Kerosene heaters](#guides/skill_kerosene_heater).
- A natural gas fireplace can keep you warm in an outage, with its vent clear of snow and the CO alarm working. A gas range can cook but must not be used to heat the room (Get Prepared outages). See [Gas without power](#guides/reference_gas_without_power) and [Natural gas safety](#guides/safety_natural_gas).
- An open fireplace: [Fireplace heating](#guides/skill_fireplace_heating). Cooking inside: [Cooking indoors](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors).

## Batteries in the warm room

- **Flooded lead-acid** (with filler caps) gives off hydrogen while charging. It is explosive at 4.1 to 72% in air, so keep flames, sparks and heat away (CCOHS battery charging). Hydrogen rises and pockets at high enclosed points (DesignSpark lead-acid). Charge these in a box vented at the top, out of the sleeping room. See [Lead-acid safety](#guides/safety_lead_acid).
- **Sealed AGM or gel** needs no topping up (CCOHS battery charging), but even sealed lead-acid can vent gas, so never shut one in an airtight box (DesignSpark lead-acid). If a lead-acid battery has to be in the living room, this is the type, but that is our judgement, not a source's: keep it away from beds, on a charger that stops at full.
- **Lithium:** charge on a hard surface where heat can escape, away from the exit and the way through the room, with a smoke alarm where you charge, and never while you sleep (LFB charging). Not on a bed or couch, and keep spare batteries away from anything that burns (Toronto lithium). Check the pack's charging range on its label, and don't charge a cold battery: one maker allows charging only between +5 and +50 °C (Victron LiFePO4). Let a cold pack warm up in the room first. See [Lithium fire risk](#browse/hazards/li_fire) and [Swollen lithium](#guides/safety_swollen_lithium).

## The rest of the house: pipes

- If the rest of the house will freeze, drain the plumbing, and learn where to shut off the water (Get Prepared outages).
- Manitoba Health says to keep the thermostat at 12 °C (55 °F) or higher so pipes don't freeze (Manitoba cold). If you're keeping some heat there, let taps drip and open the cupboard doors under sinks (CDC winter, Simcoe Muskoka).
- Thaw a frozen pipe slowly with warm air, never with a torch (Simcoe Muskoka).

## Every day

- Read the thermometer morning and night, and check on anyone at risk: see [Hypothermia indoors](#guides/reference_indoor_cold).
- Check the alarms have power. Clear snow from the exit door, the opening window, every vent and the chimney top.
- Check fuel and firewood: [What to burn](#guides/reference_what_to_burn), [Firewood](#guides/skill_firewood).
